Study Resource — Multiverse 3D XR Learning Platform

Grounded in: Unity — Introduction to XR: VR, AR, and MR Foundations (Coursera)



Learning Objectives

Define Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), and Mixed Reality (MR) and explain what separates them.

Identify the two historical products that moved VR and AR from research labs into mainstream use.

Explain what AR and MR share with VR technologically, and what makes each unique.

What XR Actually Means

XR (Extended Reality) is the umbrella term Unity's course uses to describe Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, and Mixed Reality together, because all three rely on an overlapping stack of tracking, display, and input technologies. Rather than teaching the three as separate subjects, the course explains XR chronologically: it walks through the specific hardware and software breakthroughs that let each format reach ordinary consumers, and shows how the underlying technology (tracking, rendering, sensors) is what actually differs between them, not a totally separate toolset.

Learners are pointed toward two industry-defining moments as anchors for the whole topic. Google Cardboard is used to explain how VR was made accessible: a low-cost cardboard viewer paired with an ordinary smartphone screen suddenly let anyone experience stereoscopic, head-tracked VR without a dedicated headset, and it shipped with an SDK for Unity that let developers build for it easily. Pokémon GO is used as the AR equivalent: it took camera-based, GPS-anchored AR and put it in tens of millions of pockets, proving that AR did not need a headset to be mainstream — a phone screen with a live camera feed was enough.

VR vs AR vs MR

Virtual Reality replaces the user's visual field entirely with a synthetic environment — there is no live camera feed and no real-world reference; the user is fully inside the simulated scene.

Augmented Reality overlays virtual content on top of a live view of the real world, typically through a phone or tablet camera. The real environment stays visible and the virtual object is composited into it.

Mixed Reality goes a step further than AR: virtual content doesn't just sit on top of the camera feed, it responds to and interacts with the real environment (for example, resting convincingly on a real table, or being occluded by a real wall). MR shares AR's live-camera foundation but adds a deeper layer of environmental understanding, which is why the course treats MR as sharing technology with both VR (rendering, head/device tracking) and AR (camera-based environment sensing).

Code Concepts & Examples

These snippets illustrate the underlying idea in plain JavaScript / React Three Fiber, the same environment used by the platform's in-browser editor. They are simplified teaching examples, not the completion-check solution itself.

Toggling between a VR view and an AR view

The scene keeps a single boolean flag; the environment grid group is only shown when the flag is true, which is the core idea behind an 'AR view has a real-world reference, VR view does not.'

function ARVRToggle() {

  const [isARView, setIsARView] = useState(false);

 

  return (

    <group>

      {/* The floating object always renders — present in both modes */}

      <mesh position={[-1.5, 1, 0]} onClick={() => selectObject('vrObject')}>

        <sphereGeometry args={[0.4, 32, 32]} />

        <meshStandardMaterial color="skyblue" />

      </mesh>

 

      {/* The anchored object + ground grid only render in AR view */}

      {isARView && (

        <group>

          <gridHelper args={[10, 10]} />

          <mesh position={[1.5, 0.4, 0]} onClick={() => selectObject('arObject')}>

            <boxGeometry args={[0.8, 0.8, 0.8]} />

            <meshStandardMaterial color="orange" />

          </mesh>

        </group>

      )}

    </group>

  );

}



Key Terms

VR (Virtual Reality)

A fully synthetic visual experience with no live view of the real environment.

AR (Augmented Reality)

Virtual content composited on top of a live camera feed of the real world.

MR (Mixed Reality)

AR that also understands and interacts with real-world geometry (occlusion, physical anchoring), not just overlays on top of it.

Google Cardboard

A low-cost stereoscopic VR viewer that used an ordinary smartphone as the display and sensor, credited with mainstreaming consumer VR.

Pokémon GO

A location-based mobile AR game credited with mainstreaming camera-based AR for a mass audience.



Common Pitfalls

Confusing 'no environment shown' with 'no environment exists' — VR headsets still track the real world for head motion; what's absent is a live camera feed composited into the view, not real-world tracking itself.

Assuming MR is just 'AR with nicer graphics.' The distinguishing factor is that MR content responds to real geometry (occlusion, physical resting contact), not just visual fidelity.

How This Grounds the Module's Visualization & Task

Module 1's visualization puts two objects in the same 3D scene — one floating with no ground reference (representing the VR case, where there is no real-world anchor at all) and one anchored to a visible ground grid (representing the AR case, where content is composited onto a sensed real surface). Toggling between a 'VR view' (object only) and an 'AR view' (object plus environment grid) lets a learner directly experience the core distinction the source course spends its first weeks building up to: VR has no real-world reference frame, while AR's defining feature is that its content is registered against one.

The click task (click the floating object, then the anchored object) is intentionally simple — its purpose is to make sure the learner has correctly identified which object corresponds to which paradigm before later modules build motion tracking, anchoring, and plane classification on top of this foundation.

Grounded in: Google ARCore Fundamentals — Anchors & Environmental Understanding



Learning Objectives

Explain why unanchored virtual content drifts in AR.

Define what an anchor is and how it locks content relative to the real world.

Connect parent-child relationships in a scene graph to the same locking concept anchors provide.

Why Drift Happens

ARCore's own documentation is explicit that a device's understanding of the world is never final — it keeps refining as more of the environment is observed. Because of this, poses (positions of the camera, of feature points, of planes) can shift meaningfully from frame to frame as ARCore's internal model improves. The official guidance is blunt about the implication: every frame should be treated as its own unique coordinate frame, and raw numerical coordinates should never be reused outside the exact frame they were retrieved in.

This is precisely why an object placed in the world without any special handling appears to drift or jitter: its position was recorded against a world model that has since been quietly revised.

What an Anchor Does

An anchor is ARCore's fix for this problem. Rather than storing a virtual object's location as a one-off snapshot of coordinates, an anchor is a live reference that ARCore itself keeps updated as its understanding of the world improves — the object's position with respect to the real world stays fixed even though the underlying numeric coordinates describing that position may be silently adjusted behind the scenes. In practice, an anchor is usually created from a hit-test result (the point where a ray from a tap or gaze intersects a detected surface), and objects are then attached to that anchor rather than to a raw coordinate.

ARCore also introduces the idea of a trackable — an object such as a plane or feature point that ARCore actively continues to track over time. Anchoring a virtual object to a specific trackable is what keeps the relationship between the virtual content and that real surface stable even as the device keeps moving and the world model keeps refining.

Parenting as the Same Idea in Miniature

Scene-graph parenting works on the same underlying logic at a smaller scale. When one object is parented to another, its position becomes relative to its parent's position instead of relative to the world directly — so moving the parent automatically carries the child with it, and the child's relative position stays locked. This is conceptually the same lock-in-place guarantee an anchor provides against the real world, just applied between two virtual objects instead of between a virtual object and physical reality.

Code Concepts & Examples

These snippets illustrate the underlying idea in plain JavaScript / React Three Fiber, the same environment used by the platform's in-browser editor. They are simplified teaching examples, not the completion-check solution itself.

Parenting a box to a table (locks relative position)

In React Three Fiber, nesting JSX elements creates a parent-child relationship in the scene graph — the same mechanism a real anchor system relies on conceptually.

function Table() {

  const tableRef = useRef();

 

  return (

    <group ref={tableRef} position={[0, 0, 0]}>

      <mesh>

        <boxGeometry args={[2, 0.1, 1]} />

        <meshStandardMaterial color="saddlebrown" />

      </mesh>

 

      {/* Box is now a CHILD of the table group.

          Its position [0, 0.3, 0] is relative to the table,

          not to the world origin. */}

      <mesh position={[0, 0.3, 0]}>

        <boxGeometry args={[0.3, 0.3, 0.3]} />

        <meshStandardMaterial color="orange" />

      </mesh>

    </group>

  );

}

 

// Moving the table's group position automatically carries

// the child box with it — this is the parenting/anchor guarantee.

function moveTable(tableRef, newPosition) {

  tableRef.current.position.set(...newPosition);

}



Key Terms

Anchor

A reference ARCore keeps updated so that a virtual object's position relative to the real world stays fixed even as the internal world model refines.

Trackable

An object type (such as a plane or feature point) that ARCore continuously tracks over time and to which anchors can be attached.

Hit test

A ray cast from a screen tap (or similar input) into the camera's view of the world, used to find where that ray intersects a detected surface.

Pose drift

Apparent movement of an unanchored virtual object caused by ARCore silently revising its model of the world.

Scene hierarchy / parenting

A structure where one object's transform is defined relative to a parent object's transform, so moving the parent moves the child with it.



Common Pitfalls

Setting a child's world position directly instead of its local (parent-relative) position — this silently breaks the parent-child lock the moment the parent moves.

Treating 'anchored' and 'parented' as the same guarantee against different things: an anchor stabilizes an object against a shifting real-world model, while parenting stabilizes an object against a moving parent transform — Module 3's point is that they solve the same class of problem at different scales, not that they are identical.

How This Grounds the Module's Visualization & Task

The module's before/after visualization — an unparented box jittering against a subtly shifting background grid, contrasted with the same box locked in place once parented to an anchor object — is a direct, visible dramatization of the ARCore documentation's core warning about pose drift: virtual content that isn't tied to a stable reference will visibly move even when nothing 'should' have changed.

The task (parent the box to the table, then move the table and observe the box follow) is designed to make the parenting-is-anchoring-in-miniature idea tangible: once the child object is parented, moving its parent's transform automatically carries the child along, which is the same stability guarantee a real anchor provides against a moving, refining understanding of physical space.

Grounded in: iHappy Studios — "Unity For Beginners: 5 Common Mistakes With 3D Models"; Unity Learn fundamentals



Learning Objectives

Identify the three most common beginner failure modes when importing 3D models: pivot offset, incorrect scale, and missing colliders.

Explain why each of these problems is an asset-pipeline issue rather than a code bug.

Describe the standard fix for each problem.

Mistake 1 — Misaligned Pivot

When a model's pivot point is not centered on the object, rotating it doesn't rotate the object around its own center — it swings around some arbitrary point outside itself, and even setting its position to the origin can leave it sitting somewhere unexpected. The standard fix is either to correct the origin at the source (in a tool like Blender, using a 'Set Origin' operation) or, inside the engine itself, to add an empty parent object placed exactly at the intended pivot point and make the model a child of it — effectively letting the empty object serve as a clean, correctly-centered pivot.

Mistake 2 — Wrong Scale

3D models are frequently authored in a different modeling application with a different default unit system than the target engine expects, and the mismatch is a leading cause of assets appearing far too large or far too small on import. Guidance from both beginner and professional sources converges on the same advice: fix dimensions at the source (in the modeling tool, against real target measurements) rather than compensating with the engine's transform scale field, because scaling only the placed object in the engine hides the underlying problem — it can make one scene look right while leaving colliders, baked lighting, animations, and any reused prefab still built around the wrong base scale.

An incorrect scale isn't just a visual annoyance — it has been documented to cause knock-on issues with lighting (particularly baked lighting) and with the physics simulation, since forces and collision responses are computed in real-world-like units.

Mistake 3 — Missing Colliders

An object that is visually present but has no collider component will simply fall through the floor (or any other geometry) once physics is enabled, because the physics engine has nothing to test for contact against. The fix is to attach an appropriate collider — commonly a simple primitive shape like a box, sphere, or capsule collider for performance reasons, reserving the more expensive mesh collider for complex static geometry where primitive shapes won't approximate the form well enough.

Code Concepts & Examples

These snippets illustrate the underlying idea in plain JavaScript / React Three Fiber, the same environment used by the platform's in-browser editor. They are simplified teaching examples, not the completion-check solution itself.

Fixing a pivot offset with an empty parent group

This mirrors the 'add an empty GameObject at the logical center' fix described in the source material.

// BROKEN: mesh geometry is offset from its own origin,

// so rotating <mesh> spins it around the wrong point.

<mesh rotation={[0, angle, 0]} position={[2, 0, 0]}>

  <boxGeometry args={[1, 1, 1]} />

</mesh>

 

// FIXED: wrap in a group placed at the intended pivot,

// and re-center the mesh's local offset within it.

<group position={[2, 0, 0]} rotation={[0, angle, 0]}>

  <mesh position={[-0.5, 0, 0]}> {/* local offset corrected */}

    <boxGeometry args={[1, 1, 1]} />

  </mesh>

</group>



Correcting scale to match a target size

function correctScale(meshRef, currentSize, targetSize) {

  const factor = targetSize / currentSize;

  meshRef.current.scale.setScalar(factor);

}

 

// Usage: object was authored at 4.2 units tall, target is 1.0

correctScale(boxRef, 4.2, 1.0);



Adding a collider so the object stops falling through the floor

@react-three/cannon or @react-three/rapier both use this pattern: wrap a mesh in a physics body hook and give it a shape to collide with.

import { useBox } from '@react-three/cannon';

 

function FallingBox() {

  const [ref] = useBox(() => ({

    mass: 1,

    position: [0, 5, 0],

    args: [1, 1, 1],   // collider dimensions, matched to the mesh

  }));

 

  return (

    <mesh ref={ref}>

      <boxGeometry args={[1, 1, 1]} />

      <meshStandardMaterial color="tomato" />

    </mesh>

  );

}



Key Terms

Pivot point

The local origin of an object, around which its rotation and scale are calculated.

Scale Factor / import scale

A setting applied when importing a model that converts its native unit system into the engine's expected units.

Collider

An invisible component that defines an object's shape for the purposes of physics collision detection; without one, physics forces have nothing to test against.

Mesh collider

A collider generated directly from a model's visual mesh; more accurate but far more performance-expensive than primitive colliders.

Primitive collider

A simplified collision shape (box, sphere, capsule) used in place of a mesh collider for better performance.



Common Pitfalls

Scaling the placed object in the scene to 'make it look right' instead of fixing the source asset's units — this hides the problem and quietly breaks colliders, baked lighting, and any prefab reuse.

Adding a collider whose size doesn't match the visual mesh (too large/small) — the object then looks like it's floating above or sinking into the floor even though it technically 'has' a collider.

Using a heavy Mesh Collider on every object out of habit — primitive colliders (box/sphere/capsule) are far cheaper and are the right default for moving objects.

How This Grounds the Module's Visualization & Task

Module 4's visualization stages each mistake as something the learner sees rather than reads about: a model with a deliberately off-center pivot spins wildly around a point outside itself the moment rotation is applied, directly dramatizing the pivot-offset problem before it is fixed by recentering the pivot; a second toggle stages the no-collider vs. collider-attached comparison, showing the object falling through the floor in one state and resting correctly in the other.

The three-part task — fix a pre-broken pivot offset, correct scale to a target size, and add a collider so the object stops falling through the floor — maps one-to-one onto the three most common beginner mistakes identified in the source material, deliberately built as a checklist a learner can carry forward into any future asset-import workflow.

Grounded in: Extended Reality for Everybody — University of Michigan (Coursera Specialization)



Learning Objectives

Explain why 3D interaction design is a distinct discipline from adding a simple click handler.

Describe the roles of reachability and feedback in a usable XR interaction.

Explain how raycasting is used to determine what a user is targeting in 3D space.

Why 3D Interaction Isn't Just 'Add an onClick'

The University of Michigan's XR specialization dedicates its entire second course — User Experience & Interaction Design for AR/VR/MR/XR — to the idea that designing for spatial interaction is fundamentally different from designing a 2D interface, with an explicit focus on user experience, interaction design, prototyping, and evaluation rather than programming mechanics alone. Where a flat screen click is a single, unambiguous 2D event, a 3D interaction has to account for where the user's body and controller are relative to the object (reachability), whether the object gives any indication it can be interacted with before the interaction happens, and what kind of confirmation the user gets once it has (feedback).

The course explicitly frames its goal as giving learners a design-thinking mindset and a practical toolbox — covering methods like storyboarding, physical prototyping, and digital/immersive prototyping — for building XR experiences that account for these spatial factors, rather than treating interaction as an afterthought bolted onto a finished 3D scene.

Raycasting as the Core Targeting Mechanism

A recurring mechanism across XR interaction systems (and used broadly across ARCore's own interaction guidance) is the raycast: a virtual ray projected from a source — a controller, a gaze direction, or a screen tap — into the 3D scene, used to determine which object, if any, the user is currently pointing at. This is functionally different from a flat click because the ray has to actually intersect the geometry of the target in 3D space, and the same targeting mechanism has to behave sensibly whether it originates from a handheld controller pointed across a room or a flat screen tap translated into a ray from the camera.

Code Concepts & Examples

These snippets illustrate the underlying idea in plain JavaScript / React Three Fiber, the same environment used by the platform's in-browser editor. They are simplified teaching examples, not the completion-check solution itself.

A raycast-based hover + click, instead of a flat onClick

Shows the hover-then-confirm sequence the source material emphasizes, rather than a single instantaneous event.

function TargetableBox() {

  const [hovered, setHovered] = useState(false);

  const [color, setColor] = useState('orange');

 

  return (

    <mesh

      onPointerOver={() => setHovered(true)}   // ray currently intersects

      onPointerOut={() => setHovered(false)}   // ray no longer intersects

      onClick={() => setColor(c => c === 'orange' ? 'teal' : 'orange')} // confirmed selection

      scale={hovered ? 1.1 : 1}                // feedback: subtle highlight on hover

    >

      <boxGeometry args={[1, 1, 1]} />

      <meshStandardMaterial color={color} emissive={hovered ? 'white' : 'black'} emissiveIntensity={hovered ? 0.15 : 0} />

    </mesh>

  );

}



Key Terms

Reachability

Whether a user can physically or virtually reach an interactive object given their position and the interaction method available.

Feedback (interaction design)

Any signal — visual, audio, or haptic — that confirms to the user an interaction has registered.

Raycast

A virtual ray projected from a source (controller, gaze, or screen tap) into a 3D scene to determine what it intersects.

Hover state

A highlighted or otherwise indicated state applied to an object when a raycast or pointer is currently targeting it, before a selection is confirmed.



Common Pitfalls

Wiring only an onClick with no hover/feedback state — this technically satisfies 'add a click handler' but skips the reachability/feedback design point the module is actually teaching.

Assuming a raycast-based interaction behaves identically to a flat 2D click — a ray can miss due to angle or distance in ways a screen click never can, which is exactly why feedback states matter more in 3D.

How This Grounds the Module's Visualization & Task

The module's visualization — a raycast line rendered from a simulated camera/controller toward the object on hover, with a highlight state shown before the click actually registers — makes the targeting mechanism visible rather than treating a click as an invisible, instantaneous event, directly reflecting the source specialization's emphasis on interaction as a designed, multi-stage process (approach → hover/feedback → confirm) rather than a single flat action.

The task itself (adding a click handler that toggles the box's color) is intentionally the simplest possible confirmed interaction, existing as a foundation the next module (Hand & Controller Interaction) explicitly extends into a full reach-hover-grab-release sequence.
